But the Chaldean army pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. They seized him and brought him up to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he passed sentence on him.
The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons at Riblah before his eyes; all the nobles of Judah, too, the king of Babylon slaughtered.
Zedekiah’s eyes he put out, and bound him in bronze fetters to take him to Babylon.
The Chaldeans burned the king’s house and the houses of the people with fire, and tore down the walls of Jerusalem.
Then Nebuzaradan{e} the captain of the guard carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people left in the city, the deserters who had gone over to him, and the rest of the people who remained.
Some of the destitute, though, who possessed nothing at all, Nebuzaradan the guard commander let remain in Judah’s land, and handed over to them vineyards and plowland that day.
Regarding Jeremiah, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon issued orders by way of Nebuzaradan the guard commander:
“Fetch him; keep your eyes on his welfare; harm him in nothing. Rather, whatever he asks of you, so treat him.”
So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of Babylon’s king sent
and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard and entrusted him to Gedaliah{f} son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, to bring him home. So he stayed among the people.
Yahweh’s word had come to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard:

“Go and say to Ebed-melech the Cushite, ‘So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: Look, I am bringing my words upon this city for calamity and not for good, and they will come to pass before you on that day.
But I will rescue you on that day, declares Yahweh, and you will not be given into the hand of the men you dread.
For rescue you I most certainly will; by the sword you shall not fall. Your life shall be your booty, since in me you put your trust, declares Yahweh.’”

notes.text: Hebrew “the tenth month,” Tevet; that is, January 588 B.C. (compare 52:4; 2 Kings 25:1). The Septuagint reads only “in the ninth month of Zedekiah” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “the fourth month,” Tammuz; that is, July 587 or 586 B.C. The exact year is debated. Item for scholarly review.

Rab-saris and Rab-mag are Babylonian titles, perhaps “chief official” and “chief magus” or “high officer.” The division of the names is uncertain; Samgar-nebo and Sarsechim may be a single name or a title and a name. Nergal-sharezer may be Neriglissar, a later king of Babylon (560–556 B.C.). Item for scholarly review.
Verses 4–13 are absent from the Septuagint (Brenton). Verses 4–10 closely parallel 52:7–16 and 2 Kings 25:4–12.
Nebuzaradan, Akkadian Nabu-zer-iddin, “Nabu has given offspring.” His title, rab-ṭabbaḥim, is literally “chief of the butchers” or “chief cook,” a high military office.
Gedaliah, “Yahweh is great.” Son of Ahikam, who had protected Jeremiah (26:24). He was appointed governor of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem (40:5).

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had released him at Ramah, when he took him, bound in chains, among all the exiles of Jerusalem and Judah being carried away to Babylon.{a}
The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, “Yahweh your God pronounced this calamity against this place.
Yahweh has brought it about and done as he said, because you sinned against Yahweh and did not obey his voice. So this thing has happened to you.

So now, look: today I am loosing the fetters from your wrists. Should coming along with me to Babylon please you, come, and I will keep an eye on you; should it displease you, stay. Look—all the land lies open before you; wherever you judge it good and fitting to go, go there.”

When Jeremiah still had not turned back,{b} he said, “Go back, then, to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon has appointed over the towns of Judah, and stay with him among the people, or go wherever it seems right to you to go.” So the captain of the guard gave him provisions and a present, and let him go.
Jeremiah went off, then, to Mizpah{c} to Gedaliah son of Ahikam and lived with him in the midst of those still left in the land.

When all the commanders of the forces in the open country and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam over the land and had committed to him men, women, and children, those of the poorest of the land who had not been exiled to Babylon,

to Mizpah they came to Gedaliah—Ishmael{d} son of Nethaniah; Kareah’s sons Johanan{e} and Jonathan; Seraiah son of Tanhumeth; the sons of Ephai from Netophah; and Jezaniah, son of a Maacathite—each with his men.
Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan swore to them and their men, “Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Settle in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you.

As for me, look, I will stay at Mizpah to stand before the Chaldeans who come to us; but you, gather wine, summer fruit, and oil, store them in your vessels, and settle in your towns that you have taken over.”

Likewise, when all the Judeans in Moab, among the Ammonites, in Edom, and in all the other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed over them Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan,
all these Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah; and they gathered wine and summer fruit in great abundance.
Johanan son of Kareah next came to Mizpah to Gedaliah, along with every captain of the troops out in the countryside,
and said to him, “Do you know that Baalis{f} king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take your life?” But Gedaliah son of Ahikam would not believe them.

Then Johanan son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah: “Let me go and strike down Ishmael son of Nethaniah, and no one will know. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans gathered around you are scattered and the remnant of Judah perishes?”
But Gedaliah son of Ahikam said to Johanan son of Kareah, “You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking a lie about Ishmael.”

notes.text: The introduction “The word that came to Jeremiah” is not followed by a prophetic oracle until 42:7; the chapters that follow narrate events after the fall of Jerusalem. Ramah lay about 5 miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem and was apparently a staging point for deportation.
The Hebrew is difficult; perhaps “before he could answer.”
Mizpah, “watchtower,” a town in Benjamin, often identified with Tell en-Nasbeh, north of Jerusalem.
Ishmael, “God hears.” He was of royal descent (41:1).
Johanan, “Yahweh has been gracious.”
Baalis, perhaps “son of delight.” A seal impression reported to name “Baʿalyishaʿ king of the Ammonites” may refer to him. Item for scholarly review.

verses.text: It was the seventh month (in September–October){a} when Ishmael son of Nethaniah son of Elishama—of the royal line, and among the king’s high officers—arrived with ten men at Mizpah to Gedaliah son of Ahikam. While they shared bread together there in Mizpah,

up sprang Ishmael son of Nethaniah, and the ten men accompanying him, and cut down Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan by the sword; thus he killed the one Babylon’s king had put in charge of the land.
Every Judean with Gedaliah in Mizpah Ishmael likewise cut down, and the Chaldean fighting men found on the spot.
On the day after Gedaliah’s murder, before anyone knew of it,
eighty men arrived from Shechem, Shiloh,{b} and Samaria, their beards shaved, their clothes torn, their bodies gashed, carrying grain offerings and incense to bring to Yahweh’s house.{c}
Out from Mizpah to intercept them went Ishmael son of Nethaniah, sobbing all the way. Upon reaching them he urged, “Come along to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.”
Once they were inside the town, though, Ishmael son of Nethaniah butchered them, he and his companions, and pitched them into a cistern.
But ten men among them said to Ishmael, “Do not kill us, for we have stores hidden in the field—wheat, barley, oil, and honey.” So he held back and did not kill them along with their companions.

Now the cistern into which Ishmael threw all the corpses of the men he had struck down because of Gedaliah{d} was the one King Asa had made against Baasha king of Israel. Ishmael son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.

Then Ishmael led away into captivity all who were left in Mizpah: the princesses of the royal house and the townsfolk remaining there, those Nebuzaradan the guard commander had entrusted to Gedaliah son of Ahikam. With these prisoners Ishmael son of Nethaniah set off, aiming to pass over to Ammon’s territory.
But when Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces with him heard of all the evil Ishmael son of Nethaniah had done,
they took all their men and went to fight Ishmael son of Nethaniah, and they found him at the great pool in Gibeon.
When all the people with Ishmael saw Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces with him, they rejoiced.
So all the people whom Ishmael had carried captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went over to Johanan son of Kareah.
But Ishmael son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men and went to the Ammonites.

Then Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the remnant of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael son of Nethaniah after he had struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children, and court officials, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon.
Off they went and halted at Geruth Chimham{e} close by Bethlehem, meaning to proceed into Egypt
to escape the Chaldeans; for they were afraid of them, because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land.

notes.text: Hebrew “the seventh month,” Tishri; the year is not stated (perhaps 587 or 586 B.C., or later). Jewish tradition later observed a fast in the seventh month in memory of Gedaliah (compare Zechariah 7:5; 8:19).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “Salem” (Brenton).
The marks of mourning suggest pilgrims grieving over the destroyed temple, bringing offerings to its site.
Hebrew “by the hand of Gedaliah,” perhaps “alongside Gedaliah.” The Septuagint reads “is the great pit” (Brenton), which may reflect a different reading of similar Hebrew letters.
Or “the lodging place of Chimham”; compare 2 Samuel 19:37–40. The Septuagint reads “Gaberoch-amaa” (Brenton).

verses.text: Then all the commanders of the forces, with Johanan son of Kareah and Jezaniah{a} son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, came near
and said to Jeremiah the prophet, “Let our plea fall before you, and pray for us to Yahweh your God, for all this remnant—for we are left as a few out of many, as your own eyes see us—
so that Yahweh your God may show us which road to walk and what course to take.”
Jeremiah the prophet said to them, “I have heard you. Look, I will pray to Yahweh your God as you ask, and whatever Yahweh answers you I will tell you; I will hold back nothing from you.”
And they said to Jeremiah, “May Yahweh be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to every word that Yahweh your God sends you to tell us.
Whether it is good or bad, the voice of Yahweh our God, to whom we send you, we will obey, so that it may go well with us when we obey the voice of Yahweh our God.”
At the end of ten days Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah.
He called Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest,
and said to them, “So says Yahweh, God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your plea before him:
If you will indeed remain in this land, then I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you and not uproot you; for I relent of the calamity I have done to you.{b}
Do not fear the king of Babylon, whom you now fear; do not fear him, declares Yahweh, for I am with you to save you and to rescue you from his hand.
I will grant you mercy, so that he will have mercy on you and let you return to your own soil.
But should you declare, ‘In this land we refuse to remain,’ and so turn a deaf ear to Yahweh your God’s voice,
insisting, ‘Not so! Egypt’s land is where we shall go, where no warfare will meet our eyes, no ram’s horn our ears, no craving for food our bellies; there we will settle,’
then hear now Yahweh’s word, O remnant of Judah: So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: If you are firmly set on going to Egypt and go to sojourn there,
the sword you fear will overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine you dread will cling to you there in Egypt, and there you will die.
All the men who set their faces to go to Egypt to sojourn there will die by sword, famine, and plague; none of them will survive or escape the calamity I am bringing on them.

For so says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you go to Egypt. You will become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a reproach, and you will see this place no more.
Yahweh has spoken to you, O remnant of Judah: Do not go to Egypt. Know for certain that I have warned you today

that you have erred to your own peril.{c} You yourselves dispatched me to Yahweh your God with the words, ‘Intercede for us with Yahweh our God; all that Yahweh our God declares, report to us, and we will carry it out.’
I have declared it to you today, but you have not obeyed the voice of Yahweh your God in anything he sent me to tell you.
Now therefore know for certain that you will die by sword, famine, and plague in the place where you desire to go to sojourn.”

notes.text: The Septuagint reads “Azarias the son of Maasæas” (Brenton); compare 43:2, where the Hebrew has Azariah son of Hoshaiah.
Or “for I grieve over the calamity.” Hebrew niḥamti expresses a change of heart; it is often rendered “repent” or “regret.”
Or “you have deceived yourselves”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text: When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of Yahweh their God, with which Yahweh their God had sent him to them,

Azariah son of Hoshaiah and Johanan son of Kareah, with every arrogant man among them, retorted to Jeremiah, “Falsehood is what you are telling! Yahweh our God never sent you with the words, ‘Do not enter Egypt to live as aliens there.’
No—it is Baruch son of Neriah stirring you up against us, so as to put us in Chaldean hands, to be killed or deported to Babylon.”
So Johanan son of Kareah, all the commanders of the forces, and all the people did not obey the voice of Yahweh to stay in the land of Judah.
Rather, Johanan son of Kareah, along with every troop captain, gathered up all Judah’s remnant—those who had come home from every nation where they had been scattered to dwell in Judah’s land—

men, women, children, the king’s daughters, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, as well as Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah—
and they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of Yahweh. And they came as far as Tahpanhes.{a}
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes:
“Take in your hand some large stones and hide them in the mortar{b} in the brick terrace at the entrance to Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah,

and say to them, ‘So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: Look, I am sending for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, my servant,{c} and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.
He will come and strike the land of Egypt: those destined for death, to death; those for captivity, to captivity; those for the sword, to the sword.

I{d} will kindle a fire in the temples of Egypt’s gods, and he will burn them and carry them away captive. He will wrap himself in the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his cloak, and he will go out from there in peace.
He will shatter the obelisks{e} of Beth-shemesh in the land of Egypt, and the temples of Egypt’s gods he will burn with fire.’”

notes.text: Tahpanhes, a fortress city in the eastern Nile Delta, commonly identified with Tell Defenneh (Greek Daphnae).

Hebrew malet, found only here; the meaning is uncertain (“mortar,” “clay,” or “pavement”). The Septuagint reads only “hide them in the entrance, at the gate of the house of Pharaoh” (Brenton, modernized).
The Septuagint lacks “my servant” (Brenton).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and other ancient versions read “He will kindle” (Brenton: “he shall kindle”).

Hebrew matstsevoth, “standing stones, pillars.” Beth-shemesh, “house of the sun,” is Heliopolis (Egyptian On), the city of the sun god; the Septuagint reads “the pillars of Heliopolis that are in On” (Brenton).

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans dwelling in the land of Egypt, living at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis,{a} and in the land of Pathros:{b}
“So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: You yourselves have seen all the calamity I brought on Jerusalem and on every town of Judah. Look, today they lie in ruins, with no one living in them,
because of the wickedness they committed to provoke me, going off to burn incense and serve other gods whom they had not known—neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.
Yet I sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising early and sending, to say, ‘Oh, do not do this detestable thing that I hate!’
But they did not listen or turn their ear, to turn from their wickedness and stop burning incense to other gods.
So my wrath and my anger poured forth and blazed in the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a ruin and a desolation, as they are this day.

“And now so says Yahweh, God of Armies, God of Israel: Why are you doing great harm to your own souls, cutting off from yourselves man and woman, child and infant, from the midst of Judah, so as to leave yourselves no remnant?

Why do you provoke me with the works of your hands, burning incense to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to sojourn, so that you are cut off and become a curse and a reproach among all the nations of the earth?

Have you forgotten the wicked deeds of your fathers, the wicked deeds of the kings of Judah, the wicked deeds of their wives,{c} your own wicked deeds, and the wicked deeds of your wives, committed in the land of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem?
To this day they have not humbled themselves, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.
“Therefore so says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: Look, I am setting my face against you for calamity, to cut off all Judah.

I will take the remnant of Judah who set their faces to go to the land of Egypt to sojourn there, and in the land of Egypt they will all come to an end: by sword they will fall, by famine they will be consumed, from the least to the greatest; by sword and by famine they will die, and they will become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a reproach.
I will punish those who live in the land of Egypt as I punished Jerusalem, with sword, famine, and plague,

so that of the remnant of Judah who came to sojourn in the land of Egypt none will escape or survive to return to the land of Judah, to which they long to return and dwell; for they will not return, except some fugitives.”{d}
Every man aware that his wife was offering incense to other gods, every woman present—a vast gathering—and the whole populace dwelling in Egypt’s land, in Pathros, made reply to Jeremiah:
“As for the word you have spoken to us in Yahweh’s name, we will not listen to you.

Rather, we will certainly do everything we have vowed: burn incense to the Queen of Heaven{e} and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem. Then we had plenty of food, and we were well off and saw no calamity.
But since we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by sword and by famine.”

The women added,{f} “And when we were offering incense to Heaven’s Queen and pouring libations to her—was it apart from our husbands that we baked her cakes stamped with her likeness{g} and poured libations to her?”
To the whole people—men, women, every one of them who had replied in this way—Jeremiah then spoke:

“The incense that you burned in the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land—did not Yahweh remember it? Did it not come into his mind?
Yahweh could no longer bear it, because of your evil deeds and the abominations you committed. So your land became a ruin, a desolation, and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is this day.

Because you burned incense and sinned against Yahweh and did not obey the voice of Yahweh or walk in his law, his statutes, and his testimonies, therefore this calamity has come upon you, as at this day.”
Jeremiah said further to all the people and all the women, “Hear Yahweh’s word, all Judah who are in the land of Egypt:

So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: You and your wives have spoken with your mouths and fulfilled it with your hands, saying, ‘We will surely carry out the vows we have made, to burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and pour out drink offerings to her.’ Go ahead, then: confirm your vows and perform your vows!

Therefore hear Yahweh’s word, all Judah who live in the land of Egypt: Look, I have sworn by my great name, says Yahweh, that my name shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, ‘As the Lord Yahweh lives.’
Look, I am watching over them for calamity and not for good. All the men of Judah in the land of Egypt will come to an end by sword and by famine until they are wholly gone.

Those who escape the sword will return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number, and all the remnant of Judah who came to the land of Egypt to sojourn will know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.
And this will be the sign for you, declares Yahweh, that I will punish you in this place, so that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for calamity:

So says Yahweh: Look, I am giving Pharaoh Hophra{h} king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, his enemy, who sought his life.”

notes.text: Hebrew Noph, Memphis, the old capital of Lower Egypt near modern Cairo.
Pathros, Upper (southern) Egypt.
Hebrew “his wives”; the Septuagint reads “of your princes” (Brenton). Item for scholarly review.
Verses 1–14 are a sermon after the pattern of 7:1–15 and 11:1–17.

Probably the goddess Ishtar or Astarte (compare 7:18). The Hebrew vowels read melekheth, “work” or “handiwork,” perhaps a scribal attempt to avoid the title; many Hebrew manuscripts read malkath, “queen.”
The Hebrew lacks this clause; it is supplied because the speakers are the women (“our husbands”). Some ancient witnesses are reported to include it; Brenton does not.
Or “to portray her,” perhaps cakes in the shape of the goddess or stamped with her image.
Hophra, Egyptian Wahibre (Greek Apries), Pharaoh 589–570 B.C. He was overthrown in a revolt and later killed. The Septuagint calls him “Uaphres” (Brenton).

verses.text: The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at Jeremiah’s dictation, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah:{a}
“So says Yahweh, God of Israel, concerning you, Baruch:
You said, ‘Woe is me! For Yahweh has added sorrow to my pain; I am worn out with my groaning, and rest I do not find.’
Thus you shall say to him: ‘So says Yahweh: Look, what I have built I am tearing down, and what I have planted I am uprooting—that is, the whole land.{b}
And you—great things you are hunting for yourself? Hunt them not. For look, upon all flesh I am bringing disaster, declares Yahweh; but your life I will hand you as booty wherever you may go.’”

notes.text: That is, 605–604 B.C., the year of chapter 36; this short word to Baruch is placed out of chronological order. In the Septuagint it stands at the end of the material corresponding to chapter 44 (Brenton 51:31–35).
The Septuagint lacks “that is, the whole land” (Brenton 51:34).

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations.{a}

About Egypt. Concerning the army of Pharaoh Neco{b} king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish,{c} and which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah:

“Make ready buckler and shield,
and advance to battle!

Let not the swift flee,
nor the warrior escape;
in the north, by the river Euphrates,
they have stumbled and fallen.

“Who is this, swelling like the Nile,
like streams with heaving waters?

Egypt swells like the Nile,
like streams with heaving waters.
‘Up I will surge,’ he said; ‘the earth I will flood;
towns and their townsfolk I will wipe out.’

That day belongs to the Lord Yahweh of Armies,
a day of vengeance, to avenge himself on his foes.
The sword will devour and be sated
and drink its fill of their blood;
for the Lord Yahweh of Armies holds a sacrifice
in the north country by the river Euphrates.

Go up to Gilead and get balm,
O virgin daughter of Egypt!
In vain you have multiplied remedies;
there is no new skin for you.
The word that Yahweh spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt:

Why has your mighty one been swept away?{f}
He did not stand, because Yahweh thrust him down.

There they cried out, ‘Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise;
he has let the appointed time go by.’{g}

As I live, declares the King,
whose name is Yahweh of Armies,
like Tabor among the mountains,
like Carmel by the sea, one will come.

Pack your bags for exile,
you who dwell there, daughter of Egypt!
For Memphis will become a waste,
a ruin without inhabitant.

“A beautiful heifer is Egypt,
but a gadfly from the north has come—it has come!

They will cut down her forest, declares Yahweh,
impenetrable though it is,
for they are more than locusts;
they are without number.

The daughter of Egypt is put to shame;
she is given into the hand of a people from the north.”
Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel, says: “Look, I am bringing punishment on Amon of No,{i} and on Pharaoh, and on Egypt with her gods and her kings, on Pharaoh and on those who trust in him.
I will give them into the hand of those who seek their life, into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and his officers. Afterward Egypt will be inhabited as in days of old, declares Yahweh.{j}

You, fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares Yahweh,
for I am with you.
I will make a full end of all the nations
to which I have driven you,
but of you I will not make a full end.
I will chasten you in just measure,
and will by no means leave you unpunished.”{k}

notes.text: Verse 1 heads the oracles against the nations (chapters 46–51). It is absent from the Septuagint (Brenton), which places these oracles after 25:13, in a different order (Elam, Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Edom, Ammon, Kedar, Damascus, Moab), in Brenton’s numbering 25:14 through chapter 31 (see the introduction to Jeremiah).
Neco II, Pharaoh 610–595 B.C. (compare 2 Kings 23:29–35).
Carchemish, on the upper Euphrates, where Nebuchadnezzar defeated the Egyptian army in 605 B.C. The Septuagint reads “Charmis” (Brenton).
Hebrew magor missaviv; compare 6:25; 20:3, 10.
Cush is the upper Nile region; Put probably Libya; the Ludim perhaps Lydians or an African people.

The Hebrew word division is uncertain. The Septuagint divides the letters differently and reads “Why has Apis fled from you? Your choice calf has not remained” (Brenton, modernized), a reference to the sacred bull of Memphis. Item for scholarly review.
Hebrew shaʾon heʿevir hammoʿed, a pun on Pharaoh’s name or title. The Septuagint transliterates: “Saon esbeie moed” (Brenton).
Hebrew “her voice goes like the serpent,” perhaps the hiss of a snake fleeing the woodcutters.
Amon was the chief god of No (Thebes) in Upper Egypt. The Septuagint reads “Ammon her son” (Brenton).
Verse 26 is absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).
Verses 27–28 nearly repeat 30:10–11. Here the Septuagint has them (Brenton 26:27–28).

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck Gaza:{a}

So says Yahweh:
“Look, waters are rising out of the north,
becoming a torrent in flood;
they will overflow the land and all that fills it,
the city and those who dwell in it.
Men will cry out,
and every inhabitant of the land will wail

at the noise of the stamping hoofs of his stallions,
at the rattle of his chariots, the rumble of their wheels.
Fathers do not turn back for their children,
so limp are their hands,

because of the day that is coming
to destroy all the Philistines,
to cut off from Tyre and Sidon
every helper who remains.
For Yahweh is destroying the Philistines,
the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.{b}

Ah, sword of Yahweh,
how long till you are quiet?
Put yourself back into your sheath;
rest and be still!

How can it be quiet,{d}
when Yahweh has given it a charge?
Against Ashkelon and against the seashore,
there he has appointed it.”

notes.text: The occasion is uncertain; perhaps Neco’s campaign about 609 B.C. The Septuagint lacks “that came to Jeremiah the prophet” and “before Pharaoh struck Gaza,” reading only “Thus says the Lord against the Philistines” (Brenton, modernized).

Caphtor, probably Crete or the Aegean region, from which the Philistines were said to have come (Amos 9:7). The Septuagint does not name Caphtor, reading “the remaining inhabitants of the islands” (Brenton 29:4).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “the remnant of the Enakim” (Brenton), that is, the Anakim. Item for scholarly review.
So the Septuagint and other ancient versions; the Hebrew reads “How can you be quiet.”

verses.text:
Hark! A cry from Horonaim:
‘Devastation and great ruin!’

Moab is broken;
her little ones have made their cry heard.

For up the ascent of Luhith
they go weeping, weeping as they climb;
for on the descent of Horonaim
they have heard the anguished cry of ruin.

Flee! Save your lives!
Be like a juniper in the wilderness.{d}

For because you trusted in your works and your treasures,
you also will be captured;
and Chemosh{e} will go out into exile,
his priests and his officials together.

Cursed is he who does Yahweh’s work with slackness,
and cursed is he who holds back his sword from blood.

Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh,
as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence.{h}

“How can you say, ‘We are warriors,
mighty men for battle’?

The destroyer of Moab and her towns has come up,
and the pick of his young men have gone down to the slaughter,
declares the King, whose name is Yahweh of Armies.

The calamity of Moab is near at hand,
and his disaster hastens swiftly.

Mourn him, every neighbor of his,
every one acquainted with his fame;
cry, ‘Alas, snapped is the sturdy rod,
the splendid staff!’

Come down from your glory
and sit on the parched ground,
O inhabitant, daughter of Dibon!
For the destroyer of Moab has come up against you;
he has ruined your fortresses.

Stand by the road and watch,
O inhabitant of Aroer!
Ask him who flees and her who escapes;
say, ‘What has happened?’

Moab is put to shame, for it is broken;
wail and cry out!
Tell it by the Arnon
that Moab is laid waste.
“Judgment has come upon the plateau, upon Holon, Jahzah, and Mephaath,
upon Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim,
upon Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon,
upon Kerioth and Bozrah, and upon all the towns of the land of Moab, far and near.

The horn of Moab is cut off,
and his arm is broken, declares Yahweh.

Was not Israel a laughingstock to you?
Was he caught among thieves,
that whenever you spoke of him
you shook your head?

Quit the towns; make your home among the cliffs,
you dwellers of Moab!
Become like a dove that builds
on the far walls of a ravine’s mouth.

We have heard of the pride of Moab—
very proud is he—
of his loftiness, his pride, his arrogance,
and the haughtiness of his heart.

Heshbon cries, and to Elealeh,
to Jahaz, their voices carry,
from Zoar to Horonaim and to Eglath-shelishiyah;
for Nimrim’s waters too
are turned to wasteland.

And I will bring to an end in Moab, declares Yahweh,
him who offers on the high place
and burns incense to his god.

Yes, shorn is every head,
trimmed short is every beard;
cuts on every hand,
on every waist sackcloth.

On all the housetops of Moab and in her squares
there is nothing but lamentation;
for I have broken Moab
like a vessel no one wants, declares Yahweh.

Shattered—how they howl!
Moab—how he turns tail in disgrace!
A mockery Moab has turned into,
a terror to all his neighbors.”

Kerioth{l} is captured,
and the strongholds are seized.
The heart of Moab’s warriors on that day
will be like the heart of a woman in labor.

Moab will be destroyed from being a people,
because he magnified himself against Yahweh.

The one fleeing from terror
tumbles into the pit;
the one clambering up out of the pit
is caught fast by the trap.
For this I will bring on Moab—
their year of reckoning, declares Yahweh.

Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab
in the latter days, declares Yahweh.”
Thus far the judgment on Moab.

notes.text: Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. Much of this oracle parallels Isaiah 15–16, and verses 45–46 parallel Numbers 21:28–29; 24:17.
Or “Misgab,” a place-name.
Hebrew beḥeshbon ḥashevu, a play on the name Heshbon (“reckoning”) and the verb “plot.” “Madmen” (a town) likewise plays on tiddommi, “you will be silenced.”
Or “like Aroer”; the Septuagint reads “as a wild donkey in the desert” (Brenton, modernized).
Chemosh, the national god of Moab. The Septuagint spells it “Chamos” (Brenton).
Hebrew tsits, usually “flower” or “wing”; the meaning is uncertain (perhaps “salt” or “a gravestone”). The Septuagint reads “Set marks upon Moab” (Brenton).
The image is of wine settled on its lees, now poured off by “tilters” who tip the jars.
Bethel may be the town of the northern sanctuary or the name of a deity known from other ancient sources.
Kir-heres, “wall of potsherds,” probably the Moabite capital Kir-hareseth (Isaiah 16:7, 11).
Some Hebrew manuscripts and Isaiah 16:8 lack “sea of”; the text is uncertain.
The Septuagint lacks the eagle image here and the second half of verse 41 (Brenton 31:40–41); compare 49:22.
Or “The towns.” Kerioth may be a place-name or the plural “towns.”
Hebrew paḥad wapaḥath wapaḥ, a sound play. Compare Isaiah 24:17–18.
Verses 45–47 are absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).

verses.text:
Concerning the Ammonites.{a}
So says Yahweh:
“Has Israel no sons?
Has he no heir?
Why then has Milcom{b} taken possession of Gad,
and his people settled in its towns?

Therefore look, days are coming, declares Yahweh,
when I will make the battle cry heard
against Rabbah of the Ammonites;
it will become a desolate mound,
and its daughter towns will be burned with fire;
then Israel will dispossess those who dispossessed him,
says Yahweh.

Howl, Heshbon—Ai lies ravaged!
Shriek, you daughters of Rabbah!
Wrap on sackcloth, keen,
dart back and forth among the walled pens!
For off to captivity Milcom marches,
his priests with his chiefs alongside.

Why do you boast of your valleys,
your valley flowing,{c} O faithless daughter,
who trusted in her treasures, saying,
‘Who will come against me?’

Look, I am bringing terror upon you,
declares Lord Yahweh of Armies,
from all who are around you;
you will be driven out, each straight ahead,
with none to gather the fugitives.

Yet later the lot of Ammon’s people I will turn back again,
is Yahweh’s utterance.”{d}

Concerning Edom.{e}
So says Yahweh of Armies:
“Is wisdom no more in Teman?
Has counsel perished from the prudent?
Has their wisdom gone stale?

Flee, turn back, dwell in the depths,
O inhabitants of Dedan!
For I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him,
the time when I punish him.

If grape gatherers came to you,
would they not leave gleanings?
If thieves came by night,
they would destroy only what they wanted.{f}

But I have stripped Esau bare;
I have uncovered his hiding places,
and he cannot conceal himself.
His offspring are destroyed, his brothers and his neighbors,
and he is no more.

Abandon your fatherless; I myself will preserve them;
on me let your bereaved wives rely.”
For so says Yahweh: “Look, those who did not deserve to drink the cup must surely drink it; and are you the one to go wholly unpunished? You will not go unpunished, but you will surely drink.
For by myself I have sworn, declares Yahweh, that Bozrah{g} will become a horror, a reproach, a waste, and a curse, and all her towns will be perpetual wastes.”

I have heard a report from Yahweh,
and an envoy has been sent among the nations:
“Gather yourselves and come against her,
and rise up for battle!”

“For look, I will make you small among the nations,
despised among mankind.

The terror you inspire has deceived you,
and the pride of your heart,
you who dwell in the clefts of the rock,{h}
who hold the height of the hill.
Though you make your nest as high as the eagle’s,
from there I will bring you down,
declares Yahweh.

See, as a lion climbs out of Jordan’s jungle
toward an ever-green grazing ground,
in a moment I will chase him off it,
and whoever I pick I will set in charge of it.
Who compares with me? Who will call me to court?
Which shepherd can hold his ground before my face?”

Therefore hear the plan that Yahweh has made against Edom
and the purposes he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman:
surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away;
surely their pasture will be appalled at them.

At the sound of their fall the earth shakes;
the cry—at the Red Sea{i} its sound is heard.

Mark it: as an eagle mounts and plunges,
so one spreads wide his feathers above Bozrah;
the hearts of Edom’s champions in that hour
will flutter like a woman’s in childbirth.

Damascus has grown feeble; she turns to flee,
and panic has seized her;
anguish and pangs have taken hold of her,
like a woman in labor.

How is the city of praise not forsaken,{k}
the town of my joy?

Therefore her young men will fall in her squares,
and all her soldiers will be silenced on that day,
declares Yahweh of Armies.

And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus,
and it will consume the strongholds of Ben-hadad.”{l}

Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor,{m} which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon struck down.
So says Yahweh:
“Rise up, go up against Kedar!
Destroy the people of the east!

Tents and flocks will be seized from them,
their tent hangings and every article;
camels they will lead off as their own,
shouting over them, ‘Dread all around!’

Run! Roam far away! Make your homes deep down,
dwellers of Hazor, is Yahweh’s utterance!
For Babylon’s king Nebuchadrezzar has devised a scheme against you,
contrived a design against you.

Arise, march against a nation lounging at ease,
untroubled in its living, is Yahweh’s utterance,
a people without door or bolt,
encamped apart from all.

Plunder their camels will be,
their droves of cattle booty.
To every wind I will fling the ones with trimmed temples,{n}
and from all quarters I will fetch their ruin, declares Yahweh.

Hazor will become a haunt of jackals,
a desolation forever;
no one will dwell there,
no human being will sojourn in it.”
The word of Yahweh that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam,{o} at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah:

So says Yahweh of Armies:
“Look, I am breaking the bow of Elam,
the chief of their might.

And I will bring upon Elam four winds
from the four ends of the heavens,
and I will scatter them to all these winds,
and there will be no nation
to which Elam’s outcasts do not come.

Yet when the final days come
Elam’s captivity I will turn around,
is Yahweh’s utterance.”

notes.text: Ammon lay northeast of Moab, with its capital at Rabbah (modern Amman). In the Septuagint the Ammon oracle follows those on Edom (Brenton 30:17–22).
Milcom, the god of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:5). The Hebrew vowels read malkam, “their king”; the Septuagint has “Melchol” (Brenton).
Or “your ebbing valley”; the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “the plains of the Enakim” (Brenton).
Verse 6 is absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).
Edom, south of the Dead Sea, descended from Esau. Verses 9–10 and 14–16 closely parallel Obadiah 1–6.
Or “would they not destroy only what was enough for them?”
Bozrah, a chief city of Edom.
Hebrew sela, perhaps also a play on the city Sela (2 Kings 14:7).
Hebrew Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds.”
Or “there is anxiety like the sea.”
Or “How the city of praise has been forsaken!” Some versions lack “not.”
Ben-hadad, “son of Hadad,” a name borne by several Aramean kings of Damascus.
Kedar, an Arabian tribe; Hazor here is probably a region of village settlements (Hebrew ḥatser), not the city in Galilee. The Septuagint reads “Kedar the Queen of the Palace” (Brenton).
Or “who shave their temples.” Compare 9:26; 25:23.
Elam, east of Babylonia. In the Septuagint this oracle comes first among the oracles against the nations, after 25:13 (Brenton 25:14–20), with the date at its end.

verses.text: The word that Yahweh spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by the hand of Jeremiah the prophet:{a}

“In those days and at that time, declares Yahweh,
the people of Israel will come,
they and the people of Judah together,
weeping as they come,
and Yahweh their God they will seek.

They will ask the way to Zion,
with their faces turned toward it, saying,
‘Come, let us join ourselves to Yahweh
in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.’

All who found them devoured them,
and their foes said, ‘We are not guilty,
because they sinned against Yahweh, the pasture of righteousness,
Yahweh, the hope of their fathers.’

“Flee from the midst of Babylon,
go out from the land of the Chaldeans,
and be like male goats before the flock.

Chaldea will be loot;
her looters will all eat their fill, declares Yahweh.

“Exult you may, celebrate you may,
you pillagers of my inheritance;
skip you may like a calf on the threshing ground,
whinny you may like warhorses,

your mother will be utterly shamed;
she who bore you will be disgraced.
Look, she will be the last of the nations,
a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.

Because of Yahweh’s wrath she will not be inhabited
but will be wholly desolate;
everyone who passes by Babylon will be appalled
and hiss because of all her wounds.

Array yourselves against Babylon all around,
all you who bend the bow;
shoot at her; spare no arrows,
for she has sinned against Yahweh.

“Israel is a scattered sheep,
driven away by lions.
First the king of Assyria devoured him,
and now at last Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon has gnawed his bones.

Therefore so says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel:
Look, I am punishing the king of Babylon and his land,
as I punished the king of Assyria.

I will bring Israel back to his pasture,
and he will graze on Carmel and in Bashan,
and on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead
his appetite will be satisfied.

In those days and at that time, declares Yahweh,
iniquity will be sought in Israel, and there will be none,
and sins in Judah, and none will be found;
for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.

The sound of battle is in the land,
and great destruction!

Ah, the sledge that pounded all the world—
hacked off, splintered!
Ah, Babylon—a thing of horror
in the eyes of the peoples!

A trap I laid for you, Babylon, and you were snared
before you were aware;
discovered you were, and gripped,
since against Yahweh you picked a fight.

Yahweh has opened his armory
and brought out the weapons of his indignation,
for Lord Yahweh of Armies has work to do
in the land of the Chaldeans.

Kill all her bulls;
let them go down to the slaughter.
Woe to them, for their day has come,
the time of their punishment.

“Hark! Fugitives and escapees from the land of Babylon,
to declare in Zion
the vengeance of Yahweh our God,
vengeance for his temple.{h}

Therefore her young men will fall in her squares,
and all her soldiers will be silenced on that day, declares Yahweh.

Arrogance will stumble and fall,
with none to raise him up,
and I will kindle a fire in his towns,
and it will consume all that is around him.

Their Redeemer is strong;
Yahweh of Armies is his name.
He will surely plead their cause,
that he may give rest to the earth,
but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon.

Sword upon the Chaldeans, declares Yahweh,
upon those who live in Babylon,
upon her princes and upon her sages!

Sword upon the babblers,{j} so that they turn foolish!
Sword upon her heroes, so that they shatter with fear!

A sword against her horses and her chariots,
and against all the mixed peoples in her midst,
that they may become like women!
A sword against her treasures, that they may be plundered!

Parching{k} upon her waters, so that they dry up!
For hers is a country of carved figures,
and over monstrous idols they rave.

As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighbors, declares Yahweh,
no one will dwell there,
no human being will sojourn in her.

The king of Babylon heard the report of them,
and his hands fell limp;
anguish seized him,
pain like a woman in labor.

“See, as a lion climbs from the jungle of the Jordan
toward an ever-green grazing ground,{n}
in a moment I will chase them off it,
and whoever I pick I will set in charge of it.
Who compares with me? Who will call me to court?
Which shepherd can hold his ground before my face?

Therefore hear the plan that Yahweh has made against Babylon
and the purposes he has formed against the land of the Chaldeans:
surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away;
surely their pasture will be appalled at them.

At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shakes,
and a cry is heard among the nations.”

notes.text: The Septuagint begins simply “The word of the Lord which he spoke against Babylon” (Brenton, modernized). Chapters 50–51 form the longest oracle in the book; in the Septuagint they are chapters 27–28 (Brenton).

Bel (“lord”) and Merodach (Babylonian Marduk) are titles of the chief god of Babylon. The Septuagint reads “Belus is confounded; the fearless, the luxurious Maerodach is delivered up” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous term, perhaps “dung pellets.”
So many manuscripts and ancient versions; other Hebrew manuscripts read “a bereaving.”
That is, surrendered.
Or “the sword of the dove.” The Septuagint reads “the Grecian sword” (Brenton), taking hayyonah as Yawan, “Greece.”

Merathaim (“double rebellion”) and Pekod (“punishment”) are wordplays on Babylonian place-names, Mat Marratim (the marsh region of southern Babylonia) and the Puqudu people. The Septuagint lacks both names, reading “Go up against it roughly” (Brenton).
The Septuagint lacks “vengeance for his temple” (compare Brenton 27:28).
Hebrew zadon, personified.
Hebrew baddim, “empty talkers,” that is, oracle priests.
Hebrew ḥorev, a sound play on ḥerev, “sword,” in verses 35–37. Some read “sword” here too.
Compare Isaiah 13:20–22; 34:13–15.
Verses 41–43 adapt 6:22–24, once spoken against Zion, now against Babylon.
Verses 44–46 adapt 49:19–21, once spoken against Edom.

verses.text:
So says Yahweh:
“Look, I am stirring up against Babylon
and against the inhabitants of Leb-kamai{a}
the spirit of a destroyer.

And I will send to Babylon winnowers,
and they will winnow her
and empty her land,
for they will be against her on every side
in the day of disaster.

They will fall slain in the land of the Chaldeans,
pierced through in her streets.

For Israel and Judah have not been widowed
by their God, by Yahweh of Armies,
though their land is full of guilt
against the Holy One of Israel.

We would have healed Babylon,
but she was not healed.
Forsake her, and let us go,
each to his own land,
for her judgment reaches to heaven
and is lifted up to the skies.

O you who dwell by many waters,
rich in treasures,
your end has come,
the measure of your unjust gain.{e}

Yahweh of Armies has sworn by himself:
‘Surely I will fill you with men, as with locusts,
and they will raise the shout of victory over you.’

At the sound of his thunder the waters overhead clamor,
and vapors climb at his bidding from earth’s far rim.
Lightning flashes he fashions to go with the rain,
and from his treasure chambers he releases the gale.

Hollow puffs they are, a laughable craft;
when their reckoning comes they will vanish.

Unlike these is Jacob’s Share,
since it is he who shaped everything,
and Israel is the clan he claims as his own;{g}
Yahweh of Armies—that is his name.

with you I shatter the horse and its rider;
with you I shatter the chariot and its driver;

Yet Babylon and every resident of Chaldea I will pay back
for every wicked act of theirs committed in Zion—
with your own eyes watching, declares Yahweh.

“See, I stand against you, mountain of ruin, declares Yahweh,
you that ruin all the world;
my hand I will reach out at you,
tumble you off the cliffs,
and turn you into a mountain of cinders.

No stone will be taken from you for a corner,
nor any stone for a foundation,
but you will be a perpetual desolation, declares Yahweh.

Consecrate nations against her,
the kings of the Medes,
their governors and all their commanders,
and every land under their dominion.

The land quakes and writhes,
for Yahweh’s purposes against Babylon stand,
to make the land of Babylon a desolation
with no inhabitant.

Runner runs to meet runner,
and messenger to meet messenger,
to tell the king of Babylon
that his city is captured from end to end;

the fords have been seized,
the reed marshes{j} burned with fire,
and the soldiers are terrified.

For so says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel:
The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor
at the time it is trodden;
yet a little while
and the time of her harvest will come.

‘The violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon,’
let the inhabitant of Zion say.
‘My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea,’
let Jerusalem say.

Therefore so says Yahweh:
Look, I will plead your cause
and take vengeance for you.
I will dry up her sea
and make her fountain dry,

and Babylon will become a heap of ruins,
a haunt of jackals,
a horror and a hissing,
without inhabitant.{l}

Together they roar like lions;
they growl like lions’ cubs.

While they are heated I will set out their feast
and make them drunk, that they may revel,
then sleep a perpetual sleep
and not wake, declares Yahweh.

I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter,
like rams and male goats.

“How Sheshach{m} is captured,
the praise of the whole earth seized!
How Babylon has become a horror
among the nations!

The sea has come up over Babylon;
she is covered by its roaring waves.

Her cities are turned to ruin,
a parched country, a steppe,
a country where nobody lives,
which no human being crosses.

Bel I will punish in Babylon,
and make him spit up what he gulped.
No longer will peoples flow to him like a river;
yes, Babylon’s wall is down.

Let your courage not sink,
nor be frightened by rumors heard around the land,
when one rumor arrives this year,
and next year yet another rumor,
with brutality throughout the land,
one ruler set against another.

For this reason, see, the days approach
when Babylon’s carved gods I will call to account;
her entire country will be disgraced,
and all her fallen will lie inside her.

Then sky and earth with everything in them
will sing aloud over Babylon,
since from the north her ravagers will arrive,
declares Yahweh.

For Israel’s slain Babylon herself must topple,
as by Babylon’s doing the slain of all the earth toppled.

“You who have escaped the sword,
go, do not stand still!
Remember Yahweh from far away,
and let Jerusalem come into your mind:

‘We are put to shame, for we have heard reproach;
disgrace has covered our faces,
for foreigners have entered
the holy places of the house of Yahweh.’

Therefore look, days are coming, declares Yahweh,
when I will punish her images,
and through all her land the wounded will groan.

Though Babylon should mount up to heaven,
and though she should fortify her lofty stronghold,
from me destroyers would come upon her,
declares Yahweh.

“Hark! A cry from Babylon!
Great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans!

I will make her officials and her wise men drunk,
her governors, her commanders, and her warriors;
they will sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake,
declares the King, whose name is Yahweh of Armies.

“Yahweh of Armies declares this:
Babylon’s wide rampart
will be razed flat,
and her towering gates
set ablaze.
So peoples toil in vain,
and nations wear themselves out just to feed the flames.”{o}

The word that Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah{p} son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign. Now Seraiah was the quartermaster.{q}
Jeremiah wrote in one scroll all the disaster that would come upon Babylon, all these words that are written concerning Babylon.
And Jeremiah said to Seraiah, “When you come to Babylon, see that you read all these words aloud,
and say, ‘O Yahweh, you have spoken concerning this place, to cut it off, so that nothing will dwell in it, neither man nor beast, and it will be a perpetual desolation.’
Once you have read the scroll to the end, fasten a stone to it and fling it into the Euphrates’ midstream,

then say, ‘In this way Babylon will go under, never to surface again, because of the ruin I am bringing on her; and they will be worn out.’”{r}
To this point the words of Jeremiah extend.

notes.text: Leb-kamai, literally “the heart of those who rise against me,” is an atbash cipher for Kasdim, “Chaldeans” (each letter replaced by its mirror in the alphabet, as with Sheshach; see 25:26). The Septuagint reads simply “against the Chaldeans dwelling therein” (Brenton, modernized). Item for scholarly review.
So the Hebrew consonants, which repeat “bend”; the Hebrew vowels and some ancient versions read instead “Let not the archer bend his bow, nor rise up in his armor.” The text is difficult.
Or “Take up the shields.”
The Medes, from northwestern Iran, joined in the overthrow of Assyria and later formed part of the Persian empire that took Babylon in 539 B.C.
Hebrew “the cubit (ammah) of your cutting off,” an idiom for the measure of a life or gain; the sense is uncertain.
Verses 15–19 repeat 10:12–16.
So many Hebrew manuscripts and 10:16; the Hebrew here lacks “Israel is.”
Hebrew mappets, “shatterer.” The speaker addresses Babylon (or possibly Cyrus); the verb “shatter” (napats) is repeated nine times.
Ararat (Urartu, near Lake Van), Minni (the Mannaeans), and Ashkenaz (the Scythians) were peoples to the north. The Septuagint reads “by me, and that for the people of Achanaz” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew agammim, “pools” or “reed thickets.”
So the Qere; the Kethib reads “us” throughout this verse. Zion speaks here.
Verse 37 is shortened in the Septuagint: “And Babylon shall be a desolation, and shall not be inhabited” (Brenton).

Sheshach is an atbash cipher for Babel (Babylon); see 25:26. The Septuagint lacks the name here, reading “How has the boast of all the earth been taken” (Brenton, modernized). Item for scholarly review.
Verses 45–48 are absent from the Septuagint, and verse 49 there begins “and in Babylon the slain men of all the earth shall fall” (Brenton).
Compare Habakkuk 2:13. The Septuagint reverses the sense: “and the peoples shall not labor in vain, nor the nations fail in their rule” (Brenton, modernized).

Seraiah, “Yahweh is prince,” was the brother of Baruch (compare 32:12). The Septuagint reads “when he went from Zedekiah” (Brenton, modernized), suggesting an embassy sent by the king rather than the king himself making the journey.

Hebrew sar menuḥah, “officer of the resting place,” that is, in charge of the king’s lodgings on the march. The Septuagint reads “over the bounties” (Brenton), taking it as minḥah, “gift” or “tribute.”

The Septuagint lacks “and they will be worn out” and the closing line about the words of Jeremiah (Brenton 28:64). The words “they will be worn out” repeat the end of verse 58 and may have marked the end of the oracle before chapter 52, a historical appendix, was added.

verses.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.{a} His mother’s name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
He did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh, just as Jehoiakim had done.{b}
For because of the anger of Yahweh it came to this in Jerusalem and Judah, until he cast them out from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month (in December–January),{c} on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem; they encamped against it and built siege works all around it.
The siege of the city lasted right up to King Zedekiah’s eleventh year.
In the fourth month (in June–July),{d} on the ninth day of the month, the famine became severe in the city, and there was no food for the people of the land.

Then the city was breached, and all the soldiers fled; they went out of the city by night by way of the gate between the two walls, by the king’s garden, while the Chaldeans were all around the city; and they went toward the Arabah.{e}
But the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and all his army scattered from him.
They seized the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he pronounced sentence upon him.
The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes; he also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah.
Then he blinded the eyes of Zedekiah, bound him in bronze shackles, and the king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and put him in the house of custody{f} until the day of his death.

In the fifth month (in July–August),{g} on the tenth day of the month—that was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, who served the king of Babylon, came into Jerusalem.
He burned the house of Yahweh, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned with fire.
And all the army of the Chaldeans who were with the captain of the guard broke down all the walls around Jerusalem.

Some of the poorest of the people, and the rest of the people who were left in the city, and the deserters who had gone over to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the craftsmen, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile.{h}
But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and plowmen.

The bronze pillars that belonged to the house of Yahweh, and the stands and the bronze sea that were in the house of Yahweh, the Chaldeans broke in pieces, and they carried all their bronze to Babylon.
They also took away the pots, the shovels, the snuffers, the basins, the ladles, and all the bronze vessels used in the temple service.

The captain of the guard took away the bowls, the fire pans, the basins, the pots, the lampstands, the ladles, and the libation bowls—whatever was of gold for gold, and whatever was of silver for silver.

As for the two pillars, the one sea, the twelve bronze bulls that were under it,{i} and the stands, which King Solomon had made for the house of Yahweh, the bronze of all these vessels was beyond weighing.
As for the pillars, the height of each pillar was twenty-seven feet,{j} and a cord of eighteen feet would go around it; its thickness was about three inches; it was hollow.

On it was a capital of bronze; the height of one capital was seven and a half feet,{k} with a latticework and pomegranates on the capital all around, all of bronze; and the second pillar had the same, with pomegranates.
There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides;{l} all the pomegranates on the latticework all around numbered one hundred.
The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the threshold;

From the city, too, he removed a eunuch who had charge over the fighting men, seven of those admitted to the king’s presence{m} who turned up in the city, the army commander’s scribe who enlisted the populace for war, and sixty of the common people discovered inside the city.
Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
And the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah went into exile from its land.
This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadrezzar carried into exile:{n} in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans;
in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar, 832 persons from Jerusalem;
in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadrezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile 745 Judeans; all the persons were 4,600.

In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month (in February–March),{o} on the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evil-merodach{p} king of Babylon, in the year he became king, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison.
He spoke kindly to him and set his seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon.
So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments, and he ate bread regularly in the king’s presence all the days of his life.
His upkeep, a steady ration, was supplied him by Babylon’s king, each day’s share on its day, till he died—every day he lived.{q}

notes.text: About 597–586 B.C. Chapter 52 closely parallels 2 Kings 24:18–25:30, with differences noted below; it serves as a historical appendix showing the fulfillment of Jeremiah’s words.
Verses 2–3 are absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).
Hebrew Tevet; January 588 B.C. The Septuagint reads “in the ninth month” (Brenton).
Hebrew Tammuz; July 586 B.C. (some date it to 587). The Septuagint lacks “in the fourth month” (Brenton). See the note at 39:2.
Arabah, the rift valley of the Jordan.
Or “the house of punishment”; the Septuagint reads “the grinding-house” (Brenton). 2 Kings 25:7 lacks the last clause.
Hebrew Av; August 586 B.C. 2 Kings 25:8 has “the seventh day.” The Septuagint lacks the clause about the nineteenth year (Brenton).
Verse 15 is absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).
2 Kings 25:16 lacks “the twelve bronze bulls”; the Septuagint here has “the twelve brazen oxen under the sea” (Brenton).
Hebrew “eighteen cubits” (about 8.1 m); the cord was “twelve cubits” (about 5.4 m); the thickness “four fingers” (about 7.5 cm). The Septuagint reads “thirty-five cubits” for the height (Brenton).
Hebrew “five cubits,” about 2.25 m. 2 Kings 25:17 has “three cubits.”
Or “facing the winds” (toward the four directions); the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew “seven men who saw the king’s face”; 2 Kings 25:19 has five.

Verses 28–30 are absent from the Septuagint (Brenton) and from 2 Kings 25. The figures (597, 586, and 582 B.C.) appear to follow a different reckoning, counting Nebuchadrezzar’s years from his accession, which explains why the “eighteenth year” here corresponds to the “nineteenth year” of verse 12.
Hebrew Adar; March 561 B.C. 2 Kings 25:27 has “the twenty-seventh day”; the Septuagint here reads “the four and twentieth day” (Brenton).
Evil-merodach, Babylonian Amel-Marduk, “man of Marduk,” son of Nebuchadrezzar (562–560 B.C.). The Septuagint spells it “Ulaemadachar” and adds that he “shaved him” (Brenton).

The book closes with Jehoiachin alive and honored in exile, a quiet sign of hope for the line of David. The Septuagint ends with “until the day when he died” (Brenton), lacking “all the days of his life”; compare 2 Kings 25:30.
